speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the specific activities or positions that seem to trigger these episodes of stridor and wheezing?

speaker: Patient
text: 10-month-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes of stridor and wheezing. The mother notes that the wheezing exacerbates when the child is crying, feeding, and when his neck is flexed. Additionally, there are instances where the child vomits after feeding.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do these symptoms improve when the child is supine or when his neck is extended? I would also like to know if there is a history of respiratory infections or if the stridor is biphasic. REQUEST TEST: Neck_X-Ray

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Recurrent episodes of stridor and wheezing. I also have Exacerbation during crying, Exacerbation during feeding, Exacerbation with neck flexion, Relief with neck extension, Occasional vomiting post-feeding. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Multiple sclerosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: Multiple sclerosis is exceptionally rare in infants and does not present with these mechanical airway symptoms; this sounds much more like a structural airway issue such as vascular ring or laryngomalacia. I need to visualize the airway anatomy to confirm the diagnosis. REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. Born full term with no complications during birth. Social history: First child in the family. Lives with both parents. No exposure to smoking or pets in the household.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the classic presentation of stridor exacerbated by feeding and neck flexion with relief on extension, I suspect a vascular ring compressing the trachea and esophagus. To confirm this structural anomaly and rule out other causes, I need detailed imaging of the thoracic vasculature. REQUEST TEST: CT_Angiography_of_the_Chest

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: CT Angiography of the chest confirms a double aortic arch forming a vascular ring. The aortic arches are seen encircling the trachea and esophagus, causing significant posterior and left lateral compression of the trachea and anterior compression of the esophagus. There is no evidence of aortic coarctation or other associated cardiovascular anomalies.

speaker: Doctor
text: The CT angiography confirms a double aortic arch forming a vascular ring, which explains the stridor and feeding difficulties. DIAGNOSIS READY: Double Aortic Arch
